html:
The Twelve Tables were the first written laws of Rome, drawn up by a board of ten men in 451 and 450 BCE and put on display in the Forum. They are the foundation of Roman law.

Before them the law was unwritten and kept by patrician priests and magistrates. The plebeians, the common citizens, pushed for written rules that anyone could read; this was an early round of the Conflict of the Orders. Roman tradition says envoys went to Greece to study the laws of Solon first.

The laws were short and blunt. They covered debt, property, family, inheritance, injuries and funerals. A creditor could seize a debtor who did not pay, and a father held great power over his children. One clause banned marriage between patricians and plebeians; it was repealed a few years later.

The original tablets are lost, perhaps in the Gallic sack of Rome. The text is known from quotations by later writers. Cicero remembered learning them by heart as a boy. Later laws such as the Licinio-Sextian laws and the Lex Hortensia built on them, and the tradition they began ended in Justinian's Digest.
sum: The Twelve Tables were the first written laws of Rome, drawn up by a board of ten men in 451 and 450 BCE and put on display in the Forum. They are the foundation of Roman law.
